articles.body:
Tories and Reform UK accuse Mahmood of surrendering to 'open-borders Labour left'

Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, is already ridiculing the indefinite leave to remain (ILR) announcement coming this afternoon. In a post on social media, he claimed that she was surrendering to “the open-borders Labour left”.

Later today the government will announce their u-turn on ILR, or Indefinite Leave to Remain.

It’s clear Shabana Mahmood has been forced to surrender to Angela Rayner and the open-borders Labour left. She will now allow hundreds of thousands of low-wage and no-wage migrants to stay in the UK forever and claim benefits.

By Mahmood’s own admission in a speech this March, letting low wage care workers alone stay forever will cost taxpayers £10 billion and be an “affront”. Now it looks like she’s about to do exactly that. After talking tough all year, Mahmood appears to have capitulated control of immigration policy to Angela Rayner - and Mahmood’s position is looking increasingly untenable

The Conservative plan is a ten year route to ILR, only for high wage workers. No more low wage workers should be allowed in, and those already here should be required to leave when their temporary work visa expires

Nigel Farage, whose Reform UK party wants to get rid of ILR completely, has made a similar argument in his own social media post.

The Labour Party is at war with itself over Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR), with Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood losing a fight to the far left of her own party. Tomorrow, she’s expected to cave on plans to even tinker with the ILR numbers. Angela Rayner emerges victorious, with her defence of the Tory-era policies hinging on “fair play” towards foreign nationals.

But what about fair play towards the British public? Doesn’t that count for anything anymore? Villages, towns, suburbs, and cities have to deal with the weight and strain of all this. Not only are ordinary Brits never consulted, but this current cabinet doesn’t even have an electoral mandate. It is rightly infuriating to most people who increasingly want net negative migration into Britain.

EHRC probes Reform UK over its handling of racism in response in response to revelations in ITV exposé

The Equality and Human Rights Commission has said that it has written to Reform UK with questions about what it doing to tackle racism in the party. The intervention has been prompted by complaints it has received about the racist views of some of Reform UK’s members and councillors, as revealed in an undercover exposé by ITV News.

In a statement issued this afternoon, a spokesperson for the EHRC said:

We have written to Reform UK regarding concerns expressed following ITV News’ investigation, ‘Undercover: A Year in Reform’, which aired last month. We have asked for more information including what action the party is taking to comply with the Equality Act 2010.

Following the broadcast of ITV’s documentary, we received complaints alleging unlawful activity under the Equality Act 2010, including concerns about racial and sexual remarks expressed by councillors, prospective councillors and members. As with every complaint we receive, we will assess the information provided carefully and, following that consideration, take action where appropriate.

The EHRC does have the power to launch a formal inquiry into discrimination in a political party, as it did with Labour and antisemitism. For this to happen, it would probably have to conclude that the problems were systemic and not being addressed by the party’s leadership.

In response to the programme, Reform UK claimed that the racists who were exposed were just an unrepresentative sample of “bad apple” individuals.

Green party accuses Labour of ignoring views of local leaders and voters with its Zionism motion ultimatum

The Green party has criticised Labour for abandoning local government cooperation in 11 council areas in England. (See 2.44pm.) In a joint statement, the party and the Green group in the Local Government Association said:

The Green party, and the Green group office, representing Green councillors across the country, have been hugely disappointed in moves designed by national parties to force local council leaders into jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents.

Across the country, Green, Labour, independent and Liberal Democrat councillors have worked together to provide stable local government, protect services and deliver positive change. Leaders across these parties are rightly proud of what those partnerships have achieved.

Those who issued ultimatums that destabilised power-sharing agreements have often ignored the judgements of their own local leaders, failed to respect the choices made by local voters, and are disrupting successful partnerships.

The statement did not say anything about the “Zionism is racism” motion.

Labour ends power-sharing with Greens in 11 areas where councillors refused to disown 'Zionism is racism' motion

The Labour party has announced that its councillors are going to stop cooperating with the Green party in 11 areas in England where they have been in coalition, or in some other power-sharing pact.

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, said cooperation was being withdrawn in these areas because local Green councillors refused to disown the “Zionism is racism” motion passed at their party’s conference.

In another seven areas, local cooperation is continuing because Green councillors did give the public assurances required by Labour.

Phillipson said:

This isn’t an issue of party politics; it’s about doing what is right and upholding the values anyone holding public office should share.

The Labour party fought hard to root out antisemitism within our own party and ensure it had no place in our politics. Our action is a demonstration of how today’s Labour party will not shirk from the responsibility we have to uphold those same standards in our relationships with other parties.

Last month the Labour party asked all Labour local authority groups that were working with the Greens to get a clear, public statement from those local Green parties saying they rejected the “Zionism is racism” motion and they were calling on the party’s national leadership to reconsider it. Green groups were given seven days to respond.

Having reviewed the replies, Labour’s national executive committee has decided cooperation must cease in 11 areas.

They are in these 10 authorities where there has been cooperation – Arun district council, Derbyshire Dales district council, Havant borough council, Lewes district council, Sheffield city council, Stafford borough council, Warwick district council, Wealden district council, West Devon borough council and West Suffolk council – and in Coventry city council, where cooperation was being considered.

In Runnymede borough council, cooperation between Labour and the Greens was already over.

There are seven places where cooperation will continue on the basis that Labour’s conditions were met: Broadland district council, Monmouthshire county council, North Somerset council, Rother district council, West Oxfordshire district council, West Sussex county council, and the West of England mayoralty, where the Labour mayor has a Green deputy.

The Coram Children’s Legal Centre, a charity specialising in the law as it affects children, has expressed concerns about suggestions that, under the plans being announced by Shabana Mahmood this afternoon, many foreign workers will still have to wait 10 years until they can apply for indefinite leave to remain. Anita Hurrell, head of policy at CCLC, said:

It is crucial that the government understands children’s need for permanence. Child dependants must be allowed to settle with their first settling parent. The government should keep the existing private life rules for children born or growing up in the UK so that their belonging in this country is recognised in its own right. The immigration system needs to reflect children’s belonging.

Chris Osuh is a community affairs correspondent for the Guardian.

A vigil to commemorate the lives of Africans enslaved in the transatlantic trade is expected to take place today, ahead of King Charles’ opening speech at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm).

The Vigil for the Enslaved is part of a programme of fringe events organised by the Repair Campaign for reparatory justice. On Fort James Beach in Antigua, 140 candles will be lit on the shore, symbolising the 140,000 enslaved Africans who were forcefully shipped to Antigua and Barbuda between 1677 and 1815.

A spokesperson said: “Through the symbolic lighting of candles, reflection and prayer, we will honour their memory, recognise their humanity, and affirm our collective commitment to reparatory justice.”

Ahead of the vigil, Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, chair of the all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan reparations (APPG) is expected to join senior figures in the Repair Campaign at the “From Samoa to St John’s” Chogm fringe event. The event is billed as “a frank conversation on what Commonwealth countries are asking of Britain”.

King Charles will deliver his keynote speech at Chogm tomorrow.

At the lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson rejected suggestions that Shabana Mahmood’s ILR statement has been timed today to coincide with Andy Burnham being out of the country. “I don’t accept that,” the spokesperson said, when the idea was put to him.

Asked if Burnham thought legal migration was still too high (see 9.22am), the spokesperson said it was “a good thing” it had fallen.

No 10 denies report claiming Burnham open to UK boosting payments to Commonwealth countries to atone for slavery

Downing Street has denied a report claiming that Andy Burnham is open to the UK paying some form of slavery reparations.

This morning the Daily Telegraph has splashed on a story saying Burnham is “open to increasing financial assistance for Commonwealth countries to help atone for Britain’s role in the slave trade”.

Asked about this at the lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson said:

The story is wrong. We’re not setting up a reparations fund. We’ll not be making additional aid allocations on top of existing budgets …

The position on reparations is clear: acknowledging the horror of the transatlantic slave trade and considering a formal apology for Britain’s role in it does not mean accepting a present-day financial liability.

Burnham has been strongly criticised by Kemi Badenoch and by Nigel Farage for agreeing to discuss a formal apology for the role played by Britain in the slave trade with Commonwealth leaders.

The spokesperson said that, in agreeing to discuss this, Burnham was doing “the patriotic thing”. He explained:

The prime minister wants to strengthen the Commonwealth as a family of nations with shared values that can support growth around the world through trade and economic collaboration. And as he said in his op-ed, having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do.

It’s also the patriotic thing to do, not just because it’s in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in, he said, is confident, decent, and brave.

When it was put to him that Tony Blair had already in effect apologised for the role played by Britain in the slave trade (one of the arguments made by Badenoch), the spokesperson replied:

The prime minister, like his predecessors, has expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade, and recognised the way it still shapes our world today. That is distinct from a formal apology.

We’re opening a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade, and listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state, and that will form an important part of that process.

We think it’s right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected, rather than simply deciding unilaterally what form it should take. An apology of this significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected, as they’ve asked for.

No 10 defends government plane flying from Stansted to Caribbean for summit stopping in Manchester to pick up PM

Downing Street has declined to say how much it cost for the plane carrying Andy Burnham and UK delegates to a Commonwealth leaders’ summit to stop in Manchester to pick him up (see 10.28am), the Press Association reports.

At the morning lobby briefing, asked if this was an appropriate use of public money, the PM’s spokesperson said:

The prime minister’s travel arrangements are made on the basis of security, operational requirements, and value for money for the taxpayer.

The prime minister’s travel arrangements reflect where he was carrying out official government business at the end of last week.

As you know, he spent the day in Scotland on Friday, returned to Manchester to work from Number 10 North on Friday evening. In terms of costs, travel costs will be published in the usual way.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will make her statement about indefinite leave to remain at 3.30pm, the Commons authorities have confirmed. There are no urgent questions, and no other statements. Mahmood’s statement is billed as being about “earned settlement”.

Downing Street has defended Andy Burnham’s decision to discuss the case for an apology for slavery at the Commonwealth summit.

Asked about the controversy about the PM’s comments in a Guardian article ahead of the meeting, the PM’s spokesperson told reporters at the daily lobby briefing:

The prime minister wants to strengthen the Commonwealth as a family of nations with shared values and support economic cooperation.

The prime minister, like his predecessors, expressed his sorrow about slavery - that is separate to a formal apology.

We think it’s right that a formal apology is discussed with the countries and people most affected.

A Conservative former transport minister said he took “full responsibility” after using his phone while driving, leading to a fine and six penalty points on his licence, the Press Association reports. PA says:

George Freeman was caught checking his phone behind the wheel by a cyclist who reported him to the police.

Mid Norfolk MP Mr Freeman pleaded guilty at Stratford magistrates’ court on 1 September to using a handheld mobile phone while driving, according to The Mirror.

The newspaper reported he was fined £430, as well as having to pay a surcharge of £172 to support justice services and £130 in costs to the Metropolitan police.

The MP said he had been checking a navigation app while stuck in traffic.

He told The Mirror: “I was sitting in gridlocked traffic and checking Waze on my phone. I took full responsibility and deeply regret my actions.”

Recruitment of foreign care workers on course to fall to just 10,000 in 2026/27, thinktank says

The King’s Fund, a health thinktank, is warning that Shabana Mahmood is planning to tighten the residency rules for foreign workers when the number of overseas care workers being recruited is already on course to fall to 10,000 a year.

And this is happening as vacancies in the sector increase, it says in its analysis. It explains:

Overseas care worker recruitment is falling from its high point of 105,000 in 2023/24 to 30,000 in 2025/26, with it trending to fall to 10,000 in 2026/27. In 2025/26 there were 1.02 million filled direct care independent sector posts and 65,000 vacancies. Vacancy rates in the social care sector are above average when compared with others.

Alongside a decline in the number of international recruits, the number of new domestic workers starters in care work is also falling - with now more leaving than are starting. There were 140,000 new British starters in 2025/26, down from 255,000 in 2020/21, compared with 175,000 who left the sector in the last financial year.

Danielle Jefferies, a senior analyst, said the fall in the number of foreign care workers coming to the UK would “present challenges”. She said:

The divergent trend lines of the growth in demand for care workers and the expected fall in new international recruits that the sector relies on, paints a bleak picture for where the social care workforce will be unless there is significant intervention from the government.

Foreign skilled workers eligible for ILR before end of decade set to contribute £115bn to economy, thinktank says

Shabana Mahmood has justified her proposal to make it harder for low-skilled workers, including care workers, to qualify for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) on the grounds that they will be a net burden on the taxpayer. In his statement (see 10.12am), Chris Philp referenced a claim she made in a speech in March when she said:

We have never, in the history of this country, had so much low-skilled migration in so little time. We estimate, based on findings from the migration advisory committee … That the lifetime cost to the taxpayer will be £10bn.

At the time, the Home Office published a document explaining how they arrived at the £10bn figure.

The IPPR, a left-leaning thinktank, has published a briefing today suggesting this figure is miseading because it does not present the full picture. It says:

The £10bn figure should be put in wider context. New IPPR analysis suggests that, as a whole, the estimated net lifetime fiscal contribution of all skilled workers (including health and care workers) who were expected to settle in 2026-30, along with their adult dependants, is roughly £115bn. This follows the same approach as the Home Office in calculating the £10 billion net cost for care workers and adult dependants (see methodology below for more details). The risk of deterring skilled workers who make a significant fiscal contribution should therefore be an important consideration for the final set of proposals.

Both the Home Office and the IPPR are using from a report published by the migration advisory committee (MAC), The Fiscal Impact of Immigration: Static and Dynamic Estimates for the UK. It was published in December last year and it focuses in particular on people who came to the UK in 2022/23 on skilled worker (SW) visas, and on people with health and care worker (H&C) worker visas. The report contains figures supportive of both sides of this argument.

It says that, for most categories of foreign worker visas, the people who receive them will make a net contribution to the economy over the course of their lifetimes. The only exceptions are dependant children, and adult dependants of people on H&C visas.

These calculations involve working out whether the amount that people will contribute in taxes over the course of a lifetime will outweigh the amount they will cost due to benefits claimed or healthcare consumed (or education costs, if they are children). To work this out, economists need to make assumptions about how much people will earn, when they will retire, and how long they will live.

This chart illustrates the pattern. It shows how the 2022 H&C main applicants (ie, not dependants) are expected to contribute for the next 30 years, before they start becoming a net burden.

But the MAC does say that care workers (a subset of H&C workers) will be a net burden. It says:

The H&C workers are less fiscally positive compared to UK residents of the same age (though much better than the median) – but there is still the additional benefit to the fiscal balance of having more younger workers than the UK average. We can split this group of main applicants into those who came as care workers and those who came in other health and care occupations (mainly nurses and doctors). For care workers, the lifetime contribution is estimated to be -£36,000, whilst for the other occupations it is +£166,000. Care workers are therefore fiscally negative over their lifetimes and broadly similar to the UK median for the age group.

The report also makes the point that most UK residents will, over the course of their lifetimes, end up being a net burden. But it says “because our tax system is strongly progressive, the upper end of the income distribution contribute much more than the median”. This means that, even though the average Briton using the median definition is a net cost, the average Briton using the mean definiton puts in enough to keep the system going. These figures illustrate this point.

Andy Burnham is now on his way to the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. The government plane that is taking him left from Stansted early this morning, but it went to Manchester first, where it stopped to pick up the PM. He is now en route to the Caribbean, where he will arrive this evening after a refuelling stop in Canada.

‘Was I not enough?’: care worker barred from meeting home secretary tells his story

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is due to meet some union leaders today to discuss with them her plans for indefinite leave to remain. Andrea Egan, who as Unison general secretary has many members working in the care sector, has been particularly critical of the original proposal to make foreign care workers wait 15 years for ILR. Recently she condemned Mahmood for refusing to let her bring a care worker to a meeting they were due to have about the plans.

That care worker was a Nigerian called Kolade. Aamna Mohdin has interviewed him, and he explained what he wanted to tell Mahmood.

For Kolade, the row encapsulates what he believes is missing from the immigration debate: the voices of those whose lives could be upended by its policies. He has watched politicians dismiss care work as low-skilled and portray migrant workers as a burden on the British economy.

“I was just going to tell her that is not correct,” he said. “We are not a burden to the British state. We are also contributing as much as we can, supporting British families.

“She talked about fairness to the British people. I was going to tell her that caring for British families is our own little way to show that we are contributing, and that we have earned our rights to stay in this country, a place we’re currently calling home.”

Burnham declines to say net migration still too high as Mahmood prepares to unveil tougher settlement rules

Good morning. Often these days, when the government has a big announcement and just before the relevant minister starts to give the details in a statement to MPs, Lindsay Hoyle, the Commons speaker, erupts with fury and rants and raves at the Treasury bench about how all the main points have already been leaked to the media, in contravention of the ministerial code.

Not today. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will this afternoon unveil the final version of her plans to make foreign workers wait longer before they can apply for indefinite leave to remain, and we know relatively little about what she will say. The original plans were unveiled last November and they would require most workers to wait 10 years, not five, for ILR, with care workers having to wait 15 years. They would also apply to foreign workers already here, not just new arrivals. These proposals were hugely controversial, and Andy Burnham himself was among the ministers arguing that care workers should be treated more kindly.

As Jessica Elgot and Chris Osuh report in our overnight story, there has been some sort of climbdown in relation to care workers.

But it also seems to be the case that the broad thrust of the plan is being retained and that ILR rules are being toughened in a way that will affect hundreds of thousands of people.

The detail, which is coming after 3.30pm, will be crucial; so will the reaction of Labour MPs. When Mahmood announced these plans last autumn, some government backbenchers were horrified. But mostly public condemnation was muted. At the time Reform UK had a lead of more than 10 points over Labour in the polls and Mahmood – who was arguing that net migration was too high and that low-skilled foreign workers ended up being a burden on the taxpayer (a key Reform UK claim, although one contested by experts) – was pushing at an open door.

Now the situation is very different. The electoral threat from Nigel Farage has receded quite a lot. And net migration is falling like a stone. Here are the figures from last week’s OBR report.

To implement the ILR changes, Mahmood does not need primary legislation and that means there will be no chance for potential Labour rebels to amend the plans in the Commons. But it has been reported that more than 100 MPs are queasy about what is being planned.

And Andy Burnham himself has accepted that the context has changed. We won’t hear from him until much later, because he is spending most of the day on a flight to the Commonwealth summit. But, in an interview for an ITV documentary being broadcast tomorrow, he declined to say that net migration was too high. When Keir Starmer was PM, he regularly did say this, and that he wanted immigration to fall “significantly”. Burnham told ITV small boat crossing numbers were “too high, for certain”. However, asked about legal migration, he replied:

It’s come right down. And I think when you have planned migration, it’s difficult to say is it too high or too low, because it’s got to be, if you like, following gaps in the economy.

Burnham said legal migration had “come right down”. He declined to be drawn on whether it had to come down further.

This means that Mahmood will today be defending plans drawn up in response to a problem that some might argue no longer exists. However, speaking in the Commons last November, Mahmood argued she had to do something about the “so-called Boriswave, specifically the cohort of lower-qualified workers who – along with their dependants – entered the country through the health and care visa” because some of them were “never expected to be net economic contributors”, making “more stringent” controls needed.

Here is the agenda for the day.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

12.30pm: Danny Kruger, Reform UK’s head of government preparations, gives a speech to the Policy Exchange thinktank.

2.30pm: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

After 3.30pm:Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, gives her statement on the changes to indefinite leave to remain rules.

Evening: Andy Burnham arrives in Antigua for the Commonwealth summit.

Also, at some point today Labour will give an update on how many power-sharing agreements at council level with Greens will continue, in the light of Labour HQ saying recently Labour councillors should only continue to work with local Green parties willing to disown the “Zionism is racism” motion passed at the Green conference.

articles.body:
A government-chartered plane taking Andy Burnham to a Commonwealth summit in the Caribbean made a stop-off in Manchester to collect him, Downing Street has said.

The decision, which will have been more financially and environmentally costly than if the prime minister had travelled to London, leaves him open to accusations of hypocrisy after Labour repeatedly criticised Rishi Sunak for his use of private planes and helicopters for domestic travel when he was the prime minister.

The plane, which the government leases for prime ministerial travel, left Stansted airport outside London at about 6am on Monday en route to Antigua and Barbuda, where the Commonwealth heads of government summit begins on Tuesday.

It carried officials and a handful of pool media reporters, but not Burnham. He and his wife were picked up at Manchester about 30 minutes later. The plane stayed on the ground for an hour before setting off via Canada for a refuelling stop.

Asked why the travel logistics had worked this way, and how much it had cost to add an extra leg to the trip, Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “Decisions related to travel are made on security and operational grounds, neither of which we comment on. We are transparent about travel costs. They will be published in the usual way.”

Burnham had been in Scotland on Friday, before going to Manchester to work from No 10 North that evening, the spokesperson said. Burnham, whose family home is in Greater Manchester, routinely works in the city on Fridays and spends the weekend there.

Asked if this represented value for money, the spokesperson said: “I’ve just set out our position, and I’ll just refer you back to that.” Asked if Burnham simply did not want the effort of returning to London, he replied: “I don’t accept that.”

Prime ministerial flights usually leave from Stansted, where there is a section of the airport for private flights that allows for extra security.

As prime minister, Sunak regularly used helicopters to travel to events in places for which rail travel would have been almost as quick, including Southampton, Dover, the West Midlands and Essex.

When Labour took office it cancelled the £40m helicopter contract used for the travel as part of what Keir Starmer’s government said was an effort to undo “14 years of rot” under the Conservatives.

Labour also questioned why Sunak used an RAF jet to fly to Scotland when scheduled flights were available, given the ministerial code says private planes should only be used when there is no alternative.

The shadow Cabinet Office minister, Mike Wood, said on Monday: “Labour promised a crackdown on private jet use. Yet when it comes to Air Miles Andy, it seems to be one rule for him and another for everyone else.”

articles.title: Il potere degli inquilini negli Stati Uniti
articles.summary: Le lotte per il diritto alla casa stanno cambiando la politica statunitense. E sono al centro anche del voto del 3 novembre
articles.preview: A Providence, la capitale del Rhode Island, le sere d’inverno possono essere gelide. Il 7 gennaio 2025 c’erano otto gradi sotto zero. Il sindaco Brett Smiley aveva rifiutato di aprire un ricovero d’emergenza per le persone senza casa, così due consiglieri comunali trasformarono l’aula del consiglio in un dormitorio. articles.body:
A Providence, la capitale del Rhode Island, le sere d’inverno possono essere gelide. Il 7 gennaio 2025 c’erano otto gradi sotto zero. Il sindaco Brett Smiley aveva rifiutato di aprire un ricovero d’emergenza per le persone senza casa, così due consiglieri comunali trasformarono l’aula del consiglio in un dormitorio. Arrivarono coperte e pasti caldi e una trentina di persone passarono la notte sulle panche della sala. Con loro rimase David Morales, un giovane deputato del parlamento statale. Quella notte, avrebbe raccontato in seguito, capì che Providence aveva bisogno di un altro sindaco.

Il 9 settembre 2026 Morales, socialista democratico di 27 anni, ha sconfitto Smiley alle primarie del Partito democratico. Il sindaco uscente aveva speso più di 1,7 milioni di dollari in campagna elettorale, contro i circa 500mila raccolti dallo sfidante. Morales poteva però contare su migliaia di volontari, che avevano bussato a decine di migliaia di porte; parlavano di scuole, trasporti e immigrazione, ma soprattutto di case.

Tra il 2020 e il 2024 gli affitti mediani a Providence sono aumentati di più del 40 per cento. Morales conosceva il problema anche per esperienza personale: cresciuto in California con la madre, aveva trascorso alcuni periodi ospite di amici e parenti, prima che, quando lui aveva dodici anni, la famiglia ottenesse una casa popolare. Ma la sua vittoria, ha raccontato Nina Sparling sulla New York Review of Books, è stata soprattutto il risultato di anni di organizzazione politica.

Una costante

Reclaim Rhode Island, un gruppo nato dopo la campagna presidenziale di Bernie Sanders del 2020, aveva cominciato a contattare gli inquilini della città per aiutarli a organizzarsi e trattare con i proprietari. Le prime vertenze non avevano avuto successo, anche per le ritorsioni dei proprietari e la paura degli inquilini. Reclaim ha però continuato a lavorare, portando gli abitanti alle audizioni parlamentari e sostenendo nuovi candidati. Durante uno di questi incontri, una donna ha mostrato ai legislatori un sacchetto pieno di scaglie di vernice contenente piombo, che si erano staccate dalle pareti di casa. Poco dopo sono state approvate nuove misure per proteggere gli inquilini.

Anche Smiley riconosceva la gravità della crisi, ma puntava soprattutto sulla costruzione di nuove abitazioni, semplificando le procedure per ottenere i permessi e offrendo incentivi ai costruttori. Morales chiedeva invece anche interventi immediati per chi faticava a pagare l’affitto. Lo scontro si è acceso nell’aprile 2026, quando il consiglio comunale ha approvato un provvedimento che limitava al 4 per cento gli aumenti annui degli affitti per molti appartamenti. Smiley ha posto il veto, sostenendo che la misura avrebbe scoraggiato gli investimenti edilizi. Su quel veto Morales ha costruito buona parte della sua campagna. Alle primarie di settembre hanno vinto anche otto candidati di sinistra al consiglio comunale.

Le difficoltà degli inquilini sono una costante negli Stati Uniti di oggi. Secondo l’università di Harvard, nel 2024 quasi la metà delle famiglie statunitensi in affitto, 22,7 milioni, spendeva più del 30 per cento del reddito per casa e utenze. Per 12,1 milioni la quota superava la metà. Eppure gli inquilini votano molto meno dei proprietari: secondo il Census Bureau, alle elezioni di metà mandato del 2022 ha partecipato il 58,1 per cento dei cittadini proprietari di casa, contro il 36,5 per cento di chi viveva in affitto.

Redditi mediamente più bassi e traslochi più frequenti contribuiscono a spiegare il divario. Ma può pesare anche la scarsa attenzione della politica ai problemi degli inquilini. Uno studio della Cornell university sulle elezioni nello stato di New York nel 2022 ha rilevato che, nei collegi con candidati favorevoli a maggiori protezioni contro gli sfratti, il divario era più contenuto. Qualcosa però sta cambiando, almeno nelle candidature.

Come ha raccontato a maggio Claire Wang sul Guardian, sempre più persone che vivono in affitto cercano di entrare in politica, facendo della casa uno dei punti centrali dei loro programmi. Run for something, un’organizzazione che sostiene nuovi candidati, ha dichiarato che più di un terzo dei 275 candidati appoggiati nel 2026 viveva in affitto. Tra gli eletti statunitensi, secondo le sue stime, la percentuale sarebbe tra il 2 e il 7 per cento. A Washington Aparna Raj, inquilina e attivista per il diritto alla casa, si candida il 3 novembre al consiglio cittadino in un collegio dove circa due residenti su tre vivono in affitto.

A New York questo lavoro dal basso ha contribuito alla vittoria più importante dei sindacati degli inquilini. Fin dall’inizio della campagna elettorale, gli attivisti per il diritto alla casa hanno sostenuto Zohran Mamdani, che aveva promesso di congelare gli affitti se fosse diventato sindaco. Dopo la sua vittoria, hanno continuato a mobilitarsi perché la promessa fosse rispettata. Il 25 giugno la commissione comunale che regola gli affitti ha deciso di congelare gli aumenti per circa un milione di appartamenti soggetti a un sistema di controllo dei canoni. La misura riguarda i contratti annuali o biennali che cominciano tra l’ottobre 2026 e il settembre 2027. È il risultato anche di un lavoro di organizzazione cominciato decenni fa. I proprietari contestano il provvedimento, sostenendo che non tiene conto dell’aumento dei costi di gestione e manutenzione degli immobili.

Il costo della casa sta spingendo molti statunitensi a cercare un posto dove vivere lontano dal proprio stato. Il Massachusetts, per esempio, tra il luglio 2024 e quello del 2025 ha perso più di 33mila residenti nel saldo tra chi si è trasferito in altri stati e chi è arrivato dal resto del paese (la popolazione complessiva è comunque aumentata, grazie soprattutto all’immigrazione dall’estero). I prezzi delle abitazioni sono tra le ragioni che spingono le persone a partire e la questione è entrata anche nella campagna elettorale.

Il 3 novembre gli elettori del Massachusetts decideranno se rendere più facile la costruzione di case unifamiliari, permettendo di realizzarle su terreni più piccoli anche dove le norme urbanistiche comunali oggi lo impediscono. I sostenitori ritengono che la misura favorirebbe la costruzione di abitazioni meno costose. Gli oppositori temono invece che riduca eccessivamente il controllo dei comuni sullo sviluppo edilizio, senza garantire un calo dei prezzi.

Gli spostamenti da uno stato all’altro possono avere conseguenze anche sulla politica nazionale. Il numero di seggi assegnati a ciascuno stato alla camera dei rappresentanti dipende infatti dalla popolazione. Dopo il censimento del 2030, la distribuzione sarà aggiornata sulla base dei nuovi dati demografici. Cambierà di conseguenza anche il numero di grandi elettori attribuiti ai singoli stati nelle elezioni presidenziali.

In altri stati gli elettori saranno chiamati a decidere se destinare più soldi pubblici all’edilizia abitativa. In California si voterà su un piano che autorizzerebbe lo stato a indebitarsi per 11,25 miliardi di dollari. Di questi, 7,2 miliardi servirebbero soprattutto a costruire, acquistare o ristrutturare appartamenti da affittare a prezzi accessibili, contribuendo a finanziare fino a 40mila abitazioni. Una parte dei fondi sarebbe invece destinata ad aiutare le famiglie a comprare casa. In Rhode Island si voterà su un finanziamento da 120 milioni di dollari per l’edilizia abitativa, mentre a Providence gli elettori decideranno se autorizzare un prestito comunale da 25 milioni di dollari per costruire nuove abitazioni a prezzi accessibili.

A Providence Morales ha promesso che, se diventerà sindaco, ripresenterà entro i primi cento giorni il provvedimento sugli affitti che Smiley aveva bloccato con il veto.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Americana.

“Toda la casa [por el gestor de la infraestructura ferroviaria Adif] está tensionada muy por encima de sus posibilidades en busca de respuestas al accidente de Urda , cuando aún no hemos salido del estado de shock , y manteniendo la operativa en la red de alta velocidad y en la convencional”. El diagnóstico de situación crítica es de un alto directivo de Adif que reclama el anonimato antes de una breve conversación.

Lejos de parar máquinas para analizar lo sucedido en Urda (Toledo), el ritmo frenético diario debe continuar en los centros de control . Pero son horas decisivas para el curso de la investigación del siniestro que el pasado miércoles 28 de octubre costó la vida a 69 personas en la línea de altas prestaciones Madrid-Sevilla. El presidente de Adif, Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña, tiene toda la presión sobre los hombros, al igual que todo su comité ejecutivo.

El cargo, afirman fuentes internas, está a disposición del ministro de Transportes desde el primer minuto. Y el de Óscar Puente , en manos del presidente del Gobierno. El cese de Marco de la Peña, antes o junto al de Puente, es un clamor entre los grupos de la oposición, también entre aliados del Grupo Socialista en el Congreso. Puente y Marco de la Peña, que comparecieron juntos en rueda de prensa el pasado viernes, se comprometieron en enero a trabajar para que un suceso como el de Adamuz (Córdoba), en la misma línea Madrid-Sevilla, no se repitiera .

articles.title: Pedro Sánchez: “España no se gobierna desde Washington, Tel Aviv, Moscú o Buenos Aires”
articles.summary: El presidente carga en el World in Progress contra la ultraderecha por buscar la fragmentación de Europa y reivindica su modelo económico pese a la crisis del coste de vida
articles.preview: El presidente carga en el World in Progress contra la ultraderecha por buscar la fragmentación de Europa y reivindica su modelo económico pese a la crisis del coste de vida El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha advertido este lunes del riesgo de “retroceso” en las libertades conquistadas por el avance de las fuerzas de extrema derecha y ha llamado a construir una “Europa más fuerte, más autónoma y más unida” en su discurso en el foro World in Progress (WIP), organizado por el Grupo PRISA en Bacelona.
articles.body:
El presidente carga en el World in Progress contra la ultraderecha por buscar la fragmentación de Europa y reivindica su modelo económico pese a la crisis del coste de vida

El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha advertido este lunes del riesgo de “retroceso” en las libertades conquistadas por el avance de las fuerzas de extrema derecha y ha llamado a construir una “Europa más fuerte, más autónoma y más unida” en su discurso en el foro World in Progress (WIP), organizado por el Grupo PRISA en Bacelona. En vistas al nuevo ciclo electoral europeo que se abre en el continente con las elecciones españolas del 29-N, Sánchez ha afirmado: “Ningún destino está escrito”. Y ya en clave interna, ha criticado la alianza de la derecha tradicional, que representa el PP, con la ultraderecha y ha avisado: “España no se gobierna desde Washington, Tel Aviv, Moscú o Buenos Aires”.

El arranque del WIP ha estado marcado por la dinámica electoral en la que entra la Unión Europea. Después de una mesa centrada en Francia e Italia, cuyo futuro político se dirimirá en 2027, ha llegado la intervención de Sánchez, que ha recuperado su agenda pública tras los días de duelo decretados por el choque de trenes de Urda (Toledo), que implicaron que el líder socialista aparcara la precampaña electoral. Sánchez ha recurrido a la obra El mundo de ayer, de Stefan Zweig, para describir el trance en el que se halla hoy Europa: de un continente que creía poder protegerse de la guerra gracias a las intensas relaciones de sus países a otra que se ve “destruida por el nacionalismo”. “El progreso no puede darse por sentado porque siempre existe el riesgo de retroceso”, ha sostenido Sánchez.

El presidente del Gobierno ha destacado que el mundo acusa hoy tres grandes “amenazas”: el “retorno de la guerra en Europa” con los ataques de Rusia en Ucrania; la “competencia” entre Estados Unidos y China; y la “disputa” por los recursos, entre ellos los energéticos. Esta última batalla, que ha llevado a “la guerra ilegal” en Oriente Medio, ha acarreado un coste adicional que Sánchez ha estimado en 100.000 millones de euros que ha golpeado los bolsillos y el bienestar de los ciudadanos de Europa y ha dañado al Sur Global. Ante esa situación, el presidente del Ejecutivo se ha reafirmado en su apuesta hace ocho años por la transición energética, que ha supuesto que ahora más de la mitad de la electricidad producida provenga de las renovables. “Fue un acierto, nos ha permitido ser menos vulnerables a los shocks”, ha añadido.

Después de criticar los recortes presupuestarios en ayuda a la cooperación propuestos por Bruselas, Sánchez ha reivindicado la política social de su gobierno. Tras constatar que la economía francesa ha empezado a retroceder en plena oleada de protestas, ha destacado los buenos datos macroeconómicos que arroja la economía española, con un crecimiento interanual del 2,7%, un aumento de los trabajadores afiliados a la Seguridad Social y una reducción del déficit y la deuda pública en un contexto internacional que está dañando las arcas de los grandes países del euro. “No hay que elegir entre avanzar y proteger, crecer y reducir emisiones, crear empleo y recortar déficit y deuda. Y eso mientras se reduce la desigualdad con políticas de redistribución”, ha abundado.

Aun así, España no ha sido ajena a las expresiones de malestar social en sus calles. Sánchez ha admitido los dos grandes lastres que arrastra la economía española contra los que los sindicatos han convocado una huelga general para el próximo 11 de noviembre: la vivienda y el coste de la vida. El presidente ha defendido la ley de Vivienda, de cuyos resultados ha sacado pecho este lunes el president Salvador Illa con las inéditas bajadas en los precios del alquiler en la ciudad de Barcelona, muy presionada por el turismo, en los dos años de aplicación de la norma. Sánchez ha cargado contra los partidos que se niegan a aplicar esa norma. “España está avanzando, y lo hace sin renunciar al modelo social europeo, cuestionado por fuerzas que quieren socavar nuestra unidad”, ha remachado.

El presidente ha cargado ahí contra la ultraderecha, que ha presentado como la gran amenaza interna de la UE al ser una fuerza que busca esa fragmentación que destruyó la sociedad cosmopolita en la que creció Zweig. “La fragmentación para ellos no es un medio para alcanzar el poder, sino un fin por si mismo”, ha criticado Sánchez. “La democracia y los derechos humanos no son el final de una carrera ya ganada, hay que luchar por ellos día a día”, ha agregado. Sánchez, además, ha lamentado que una parte de la derecha tradicional se haya arrimado a los ultras, acabando fagocitados por estos. Algo que, a su juicio, no ha ocurrido en la Alemania de Friedich Merz o la Polonia de Donald Tusk, que se han mantenido firmes en su cordón sanitario a las fuerzas ultras. Sánchez ha criticado, además, que esos partidos se sometan a “oligarcas extranjeros” y tejan alianzas con otros países para debilitar Europa. “España no se gobierna desde Washington, Tel Aviv, Moscú o Buenos Aires”, ha avisado.

Como ha venido haciendo a lo largo de esta legislatura, Sánchez ha abogado por intervenir en los nuevos entornos tecnológicos. “Hay una queja sobre la excesiva regulación. No es un problema de regulación, sino de buna no mala regulación”, ha señalado el presidente, quien ha puesto el ejemplo de la inteligencia artificial. “Necesitamos un marco con un horizonte hacia el que queramos progresar”, ha remachado. Y ahí el “faro” también es Bruselas. “Nuestra respuesta debe ser mucha más Europa. Frente a quienes quieren dividirnos, más unidad”, ha concluido.

articles.title: La crisi politica polacca si ripercuote su tutta l’Europa
articles.summary: Lo scontro tra il governo filoeuropeo di Donald Tusk e il partito nazionalista Pis sulla corte costituzionale ha scatenato il caos nel paese. È intervenuta anche la Commissione europea

articles.body:
Colpo di stato o ripristino della democrazia? Dopo una grave crisi politica esplosa il 30 ottobre, in Polonia (e non solo) imperversa la battaglia tra due narrazioni opposte, che mostra la difficoltà di ristabilire le norme democratiche dopo che le forze populiste sono state a lungo al potere.

Lo scontro è tra il governo centrista e filoeuropeo di Donald Tusk, ex presidente del consiglio europeo, e Diritto e giustizia (Pis), il partito di destra nazionalista ed euroscettico che mantiene la presidenza del paese con Karol Nawrocki, eletto l’anno scorso. Questa difficile coabitazione è segnata da forti tensioni, in attesa delle elezioni in programma nell’ottobre 2027.

In questo contesto di estrema polarizzazione il 30 ottobre alcuni giudici della corte eletti dalla maggioranza filoeuropea, ma alle cui nomine si oppone Nawrocki, hanno provato a esautorare il presidente e il vicepresidente del tribunale. A quel punto la prova di forza giuridica è diventata una prova di forza fisica.

Caos totale

La polizia si è presentata in assetto antisommossa davanti alla sede della corte costituzionale, dove c’erano anche i militanti del Pis. Intanto il ministro della giustizia aveva avviato una procedura per revocare l’immunità del presidente della corte, mentre il capo dello stato, in viaggio verso il Senegal, ha invertito la rotta per andare direttamente al tribunale.

Nawrocki ha denunciato un tentativo di colpo di stato del governo, che però sostiene di aver agito legalmente. Il caos è totale.

Il 31 ottobre il Pis ha annunciato di voler rovesciare il governo attraverso una mozione di sfiducia in parlamento e di sostituirlo con un esecutivo tecnico che dovrebbe restare in carica fino alle elezioni dell’anno prossimo.

Da Parigi a Bruxelles

La vicenda ha una dimensione europea. Il primo ministro si appella a una decisione della Corte europea dei diritti dell’uomo, che riconosce al parlamento il diritto di nominare i giudici. Il 31 ottobre la Commissione europea ha chiesto a Nawrocki di convalidare la nomina dei giudici.

La crisi polacca ha fatto irruzione nella campagna elettorale francese. Il 31 ottobre Marine Le Pen, candidata dell’estrema destra, ha manifestato la sua “profonda inquietudine” parlando di una “manovra forzata per prendere il controllo di un’istituzione costituzionale”. Immediatamente è arrivata la risposta secca del candidato socialista Raphaël Glucksmann, che ha ricordato a Le Pen “le violazioni dello stato di diritto commesse dai suoi amici ultraconservatori in Polonia”.

La posta in gioco è alta: i governi illiberali hanno regolarmente preso di mira la giustizia, dall’Ungheria di Viktor Orbán alla Polonia del Pis, fino a Israele con Benjamin Netanyahu. Come si fa a tornare indietro nel caso di un’alternanza democratica (come in Ungheria) o di una coabitazione (come in Polonia)? Battere i populisti alle urne non basta a ristabilire le regole democratiche, perché i danni che hanno provocato possono essere molto profondi.

Nella battaglia che nasce da ogni incidente nelle democrazie liberali polarizzate, con la Russia sempre pronta a gettare benzina sul fuoco, i populisti invocano uno stato di diritto che però hanno l’abitudine di maltrattare. È un modo per capovolgere i ruoli, incolpando l’Europa e vendendo agli elettori una realtà alternativa.

La Polonia sta vivendo un momento di questo tipo, a un anno dalle elezioni generali. Com’era prevedibile, la Francia, in piena campagna elettorale, vede nella crisi polacca un’anticipazione delle possibili battaglie tra Le Pen e il consiglio costituzionale.

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

articles.preview: Survey finds UK government’s decision to impose trade ban was not a decisive factor in how Israelis voted in election The UK government’s decision to impose a ban on trade in goods from illegal settlements was not decisive in how Israelis voted in their general election , but a majority think the Israeli government’s settlements policy should change if it is going to lead to further sanctions, a new poll of Israelis shows.
articles.body:
The UK government’s decision to impose a ban on trade in goods from illegal settlements was not decisive in how Israelis voted in their general election, but a majority think the Israeli government’s settlements policy should change if it is going to lead to further sanctions, a new poll of Israelis shows.

There had been fierce criticism of the UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s decision in September to impose a trade ban and wider sanctions on illegal settlements, with some claiming it would drive Israeli voters into the arms of Benjamin Netanyahu.

A survey last month by Israeli social research group aChord shows overall support for foreign sanctions on violent settlers in the West Bank, but there was little support for the UK’s ban on trade with goods from illegal settlements, with many fearing it would end up being extended across Israel.

The survey is unique in showing how much the tougher line on Israel adopted by Britain and some foreign states was affecting the thinking of Israeli voters, and the extent to which Israelis thought it was a response to Israel’s actions or born of hostility to Israel, or even antisemitism.

The survey showed that three-quarters of supporters of the bloc backing Netanyahu said UK sanctions and trade ban policies towards Israel did not affect their vote at all, and to the small extent that they changed anyone’s vote, they shifted voters both ways, leaving no detectable net effect.

Just over three-quarters of all those surveyed (76) – had heard of the UK government announcement on settlements, even if 18 % had only heard the broad headline. Four-fifths of those that were aware of the announcement knew that the policy applied to the West Bank, and not the whole of Israel.

Israel’s relations with the west were “important or very important” to 60% of the supporters of the Change bloc of parties backing Gadi Eisenkot in deciding their vote. But even then these relationships came fifth in importance in a proffered group of six motives for voting. Only 30% of supporters of the Netanyahu bloc said relations with the west mattered in the same way.

But 71% of voters for the opposition Change bloc said the Israeli government should adapt its settlements policy to avoid an escalation of sanctions. Only 14% of Netanyahu bloc voters agreed, most saying instead that the government should continue the policy “whatever the price”.

A plurality of the public – 50% – said the settlement and construction policy in the West Bank should be adjusted to avoid sanctions escalation and international isolation, with 71% of Eisenkot bloc supporters agreeing to this proposition. Support for a change in the policy is strongest among supporters of the Arab parties.

The finding prompted Hannah Weisfeld, the director of the British-Jewish organisation Yachad, to claim the research “illustrates that the Israeli public certainly recognises that if there is not a policy shift in relation to settlement enterprise, the international community is likely to try to create an incentive to shift things from the outside. If anything, that highlights the importance of UK and other allies taking action that targets the occupation.”

The survey also showed that concerns about foreign sanctions are highest when voters feel they will suffer a high personal price. Only 36% of all those surveyed agreed that the settlement policy should continue even if sanctions on banks that finance construction in illegal settlements led either to higher interest rates, difficulties in transferring money abroad, or using credit cards abroad. The poll suggests that the more people feel they will be damaged personally, the more they oppose the settlement policy.

A majority of all Israelis surveyed (52%) support sanctions on individual violent settlers, so long as the sanctions are imposed only on those acting violently, but 70% of Netanyahu bloc supporters oppose foreign sanctions in all circumstances.

There is much less widespread support for the policy of banning the import of goods from the illegal settlement, with 63% of all those surveyed opposing the ban and 26% either supporting the measure outright, or saying they would if it were underlined that the ban would not apply to goods from outside settlements.

articles.title: Russia's giant new radar in Kaliningrad raises alarm in NATO
articles.summary: Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff between Moscow and NATO.
articles.preview: Russia's new suspected radar in Kaliningrad could spy deep into Europe November 1, 2026 Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff between Moscow and NATO. The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.
articles.body:
Russia's new suspected radar in Kaliningrad could spy deep into Europe

November 1, 2026

Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff between Moscow and NATO.

The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.

From above, the three radiating arms of the sprawling facility, each more than 500 meters (1,640 feet) long, look like some sort of alien lifeform has left its mark on an otherwise undisturbed stretch of forested nature reserve. You could actually compare it to a landing platform or launch pad for Moscow's massive intelligence-gathering network.

While Russia has not confirmed it is building the structure, security expert Vaidotas Malinionis said the radar will be so big, it will be able to see beyond the earth's curvature. The retired commander from Lithuania told DW the over-the-horizon (OTH) radar network near Gvardeysk will have a surveillance range of about 3,000 kilometers (1,864 miles), allowing Russia to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine.

The system would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications and detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles.

"The goal and the purpose of this radar is observation of long-distance targets and early warning capabilities. We still don't know if it is operationally capable of doing that, but it is definitely being constructed right now," Malinionis added.

Mass surveillance system

The British newspaper The Times reports that the systems are primarily intended for the detection and jamming of electronic signals, citing the Finnish-Polish space and defense technology company ICEYE.

"They would be able to use it in offensive operations, to get more information about specific targets," explained Malinionis.

"And if they were able to get an early warning about the movement of NATO troops, in the case of an invasion on NATO's eastern frontier, then they would gain more time for decision-making."

Speaking to DW from the shores of the Baltic Sea, Latvian geopolitical analyst Evija Djatkovica warned there is a significant downside for NATO to this old Soviet technology being revived when it comes to the increased use of new tech in the warfare of today.

"It will help Russia close existing loopholes in detecting low-flying objects, making the rapidly developing integration of drones into regional defense doctrines less effective," she claimed.

Electronic warfare hub

The Times report goes on to say that ICEYE defense company sees Russia's expansion of its OTH radar system as proof that Kaliningrad is being developed into a hub for advanced military sensors and electronic warfare systems.

"The new radar signals an intensifying contest between Russia and NATO for military supremacy and control of the Kaliningrad region," Djatkovica underlined.

"This is a potentially dangerous situation, since further militarization on both sides could be expected and, at some point, a preemptive strike becomes an option to deny the other side an unacceptable advantage over the region,” she warned.

Russia has already alerted NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to blockade Kaliningrad. The potential flashpoint and Russian outpost is situated on the Baltic Sea, wedged between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania– on the very doorstep of the alliance's eastern flank.

The exclave is only 200 kilometers from west to east and 100 kilometers from north to south. However, from what Malinionis asserted, Russia's smallest federal region or oblast packs a punch.

"According to some sources, they have the capability to deploy up to 100 nuclear warheads in Kaliningrad. And some sources say they have already started deploying some there – although that is yet to be confirmed," the former commander pointed out.

ICEYE claims to have discovered another large circular antenna complex some 50 kilometers west of Gvardeysk, near the city of Chernyakhovsk, according to the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ). More than 20 signal and electronic warfare facilities are reportedly peppered throughout the Kaliningrad region.

Satellite images also reveal new shelters for fighter jets at the Kaliningrad-Chkalovsk military airfield, according to the FAZ report. Other images show launch pads at the mobile S-400 surface-to-air missile site in Baltiysk, meaning the systems could well be operational.

"These factors clearly depict the strategic importance of territories around Kaliningrad for both Russia and NATO," said Djatkovica. "For Russia, among other things, Kaliningrad's geographic position and nuclear arsenal stationed there allow it to project threats against most European capitals."

This is where the gargantuan radar comes into play, according to her. "Because of the radar's long reach, other European regions from North to West will also become more exposed to Russia's surveillance and military actions."

Motivation for the West

She sighed, saying the good news is that every escalatory step that Russia takes, with repercussions for European countries even further away from its borders, the more the whole continent takes Moscow seriously as a direct threat.

"Russia's malign signals should motivate the West to keep up with rearmament, which, in turn, will make NATO and Europe's collective deterrence more credible."

Djatkovica used the example of Poland, which has been transforming its offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea into NATO surveillance infrastructure.

In another step towards integrating newer technologies, German arms producer Rheinmetall is building Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in conjunction with the firm ICEYE. They beam down precise pictures of troop movements and enemy positions, even at night or in bad weather.

The images will be used on NATO's eastern flank and by the Bundeswehr brigade stationed in Lithuania. The first SAR satellites are set to be launched into orbit on a SpaceX rocket in early 2027.

Malinionis agreed that adaptation is the most important lesson to be learnt for European leaders in times of Russian aggression. But he had another point to make. "There is also one disadvantage for this new Russian radar. Because it's so huge, it's a pretty easy target!"

articles.title: La Bulgaria conferma la filorussa Yotova, battuto l'europeista Ghiurov
articles.summary: Contraria alle sanzioni, preme per il dialogo con Mosca. Bassa l'affluenza, meno del 30%
articles.preview: Cala il sipario sulle elezioni presidenziali in Bulgaria, con la vittoria al ballottaggio, in larga misura annunciata, della capo di Stato uscente Yliana Yotova, che stando agli exit poll e ai risultati preliminari, ha superato di gran lunga lo sfidante Andrei Ghiurov. Appoggiata dal premier Rumen Radev e dal suo partito Bulgaria Progressista, la socialista Yotova - favorevole al dialogo con Mosca - ha ottenuto il 58,2% dei voti, secondo la proiezione dell'agenzia demoscopica Miara.
articles.body:
Cala il sipario sulle elezioni presidenziali in Bulgaria, con la vittoria al ballottaggio, in larga misura annunciata, della capo di Stato uscente Yliana Yotova, che stando agli exit poll e ai risultati preliminari, ha superato di gran lunga lo sfidante Andrei Ghiurov.

Appoggiata dal premier Rumen Radev e dal suo partito Bulgaria Progressista, la socialista Yotova - favorevole al dialogo con Mosca - ha ottenuto il 58,2% dei voti, secondo la proiezione dell'agenzia demoscopica Miara. L'europeista Andrey Ghiurov, sostenuto dai liberali di Bulgaria Democratica con gli alleati del partito 'Continuiamo il Cambiamento', si è invece fermato al 38,6%. La percentuale restante di elettori ha invece scelto la casella "Non voto per nessuno". Come al primo turno però, l'affluenza alle urne è stata molto bassa: poco più del 29% degli aventi diritto aveva votato alle ore 19 locali, un'ora prima della chiusura dei seggi.

Yotova, 62 anni, è una giornalista e attivista del Partito socialista bulgaro, eurodeputata dal 2007 al 2017, vicepresidente della Bulgaria dal 2017 allo scorso gennaio, quando ha sostituito Rumen Radev. Questi allora rassegnò clamorosamente le dimissioni per presentarsi alle elezioni politiche, tenutesi in aprile, a capo di un nuovo partito, promettendo una lotta senza quartiere alla corruzione e alla criminalità organizzata.

Durante la campagna elettorale, Yotova non ha messo in discussione l'appartenenza della Bulgaria alla Ue e alla Nato, ma ha sottolineato che in politica estera bisogna essere pragmatici e che per risolvere il conflitto in Ucraina bisogna "ricorrere alla diplomazia e non alle armi". In diverse occasioni ha definito la Russia "aggressore" precisando però che le sanzioni Ue contro Mosca sono controproducenti e che la questione "va risolta sul tavolo delle trattative".

La Bulgaria è una repubblica parlamentare e i poteri del capo dello Stato sono limitati e per lo più rappresentativi. Il voto si è svolto in un clima di timori sociali e incertezze economiche. Dopo l'ingresso della Bulgaria nell'Eurozona, il primo gennaio scorso, e a causa delle turbolenze nel settore dell'energia, il Paese è afflitto da un forte rincaro di generi alimentari, servizi e tariffe di luce, acqua e riscaldamento. A questi problemi si sovrappone l'elemento di tensione delle navi affondate da droni nel Mar Nero, nei pressi delle acque territoriali bulgare.

articles.title: Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
articles.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro failed to gain power, Aleksandar Vucic was voted out of office, and even Benjamin Netanyahu's position has weakened. An unhappy US President Trump is crying electoral fraud.
articles.preview: November 1, 2026 Flavio Bolsonaro failed to gain power, Aleksandar Vucic was voted out of office, and even Benjamin Netanyahu's position has weakened. An unhappy US President Trump is crying electoral fraud. The midterm elections in the United States are just around the corner: On Tuesday, November 3, American voters will choose their representatives to the US Congress. The right-wing-conservative Republican party of President Donald Trump currently has a majority in both chambers. But in other parts of the world election results are already in.
articles.body:
November 1, 2026

Flavio Bolsonaro failed to gain power, Aleksandar Vucic was voted out of office, and even Benjamin Netanyahu's position has weakened. An unhappy US President Trump is crying electoral fraud.

The midterm elections in the United States are just around the corner: On Tuesday, November 3, American voters will choose their representatives to the US Congress. The right-wing-conservative Republican party of President Donald Trump currently has a majority in both chambers.

But in other parts of the world election results are already in. The majority of voters in both Serbia and Brazil cast their ballots for left-wing parties. Those results will not influence the midterms in the US, but the victories of the Student List in Serbia and the incumbent president, Luiz Inacio "Lula" da Silva, in Brazil are bad news for Trump all the same.

In Serbia, he has lost an important European ally in outgoing president Aleksandar Vucic. And in Brazil, the Trump camp had been hoping Flavio Bolsonaro would triumph.

"Trump was a strong supporter of both Jair Bolsonaro, the Trump-like figure who served as president before Lula defeated him in 2022, and of his son Flavio," says Lawrence J. Haas, a senior fellow for US foreign policy at the American Foreign Policy Council, who was communications director for Al Gore, Bill Clinton's vice president, in the 1990s. "Trump wasn't happy about the defeat of either Bolsonaro," he continues, "and he doesn't feel warmly toward Lula. So relations will remain cool at best."

Trump declared Brazilian election looked "rigged"

Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption and money laundering. After losing the election, he fled the country for Florida. The US State Department granted him and his family entry visas in spite of the pending legal action.

Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat. Instead, he claims there were irregularities in the vote. This is very reminiscent of Trump, who continues to claim – falsely – that Joe Biden and the Democratic Party "stole" the US election in 2020. Trump's comments on Bolsonaro's defeat sounded very familiar. "It looked like another rigged election, frankly," the US president said on Monday. "Elections have to be indisputable – and it looked very bad to me."

Good relations with Putin ally Vucic

Aleksandar Vucic had ruled Serbia as president with an iron fist since 2017. He resigned just before these elections in order to stand as prime minister, a role he previously held from 2014 to 2017. Vucic has commented in the past that he and President Trump are like-minded people. Trump's eldest son, Donald Jr., visited Vucic in Belgrade shortly before the US presidential elections in November 2024, and again a few months later.

The US Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), which is closely connected with Trump's MAGA ("Make America Great Again") movement, recently announced that it was organizing a meeting in Belgrade in November, at which Vucic was to be a keynote speaker. It is unclear whether this is still the case.

Another thing Vucic and Trump have in common is that the soon-to-be-ex-president of Serbia has a much more positive attitude toward Russian president Vladimir Putin than do most other European heads of state. Vucic did not join EU countries in imposing sanctions on Russia after it launched its war of aggression against Ukraine. Belgrade still buys Russian raw materials, and Serbian state media under Vucic presented a more positive image of Russia than of the EU.

Trump also seems increasingly inclined toward Moscow. His special envoy Steve Witkoff recently described Putin as a "humanitarian," while, in an interview, Trump himself openly admitted that he got on better with Putin than with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The end of the Vucic government now means that Trump has lost one of his few allies in Europe who takes a similar view.

Israel: Outcome still unclear

There's still a chance of an outcome in the Israeli elections that might be to Trump's liking. With more than 96% of votes counted, the right-wing bloc led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in the lead. However, Trump ally Netanyahu has lost his majority, and the coalition negotiations will be very difficult.

Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies since well before February this year, when they joined forces to launch a war against Iran. In 2018, during his first term in office, Trump moved the US embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. This was controversial, because both Israel and Palestinians claim Jerusalem as their capital. Netanyahu's camp welcomed the decision.

Today, the United States is still by far Israel's most important partner, while Israel is an important regional ally for the US. It is not clear what their relationship would be like with a different Israeli government. If Netanyahu remains in power, little, if anything, will change.

No rosy prospects for Trump in the midterms

With Vucic's defeat, Trump has lost a loyal ally. And Lula's victory means, for him, that a disagreeable president remains in power. None of this is good for Trump, but foreign policy analyst Haas said it won't influence the important midterm elections in his country. "Americans will be voting [...] on the basis of issues that affect them, and how they feel about the party in power."

But this doesn't bode well for Trump, either. "Trump has the lowest approval rating of any president on the eve of a mid-term election since Harry Truman in 1946," Haas explained. "Americans are very concerned about issues of affordability, [and] they strongly oppose the US-Iran war."

Benjamin Alvarez Gruber in Miami contributed to this report, which was originally written in German.

articles.title: Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
articles.summary: After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the losers still hold sway in the judiciary and administration.
articles.preview: October 31, 2026 After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the losers still hold sway in the judiciary and administration. Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.
articles.body:
October 31, 2026

After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the losers still hold sway in the judiciary and administration.

Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.

Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practicing "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."

Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.

On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.

Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."

Old accusations against Vucic

The List, which emerged from the student revolt, is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote, leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.

Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.

The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime.

The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died. The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.

Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.

"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."

Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.

How much damage can the old government do to the new one?

It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia, an organization that monitors the work of governments.

The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.

However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."

In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.

No change in foreign policy

The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.

Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.

"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.

Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.

The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.

This article has been translated from German.

Ancora una volta il futuro di Israele è stato deciso dagli arabi.
